title: Asia stocks mixed as oil retreats, earnings season gathers pace
full_text:
8 emerging markets to consider in 2027: HSBC
Investing.com -- Asian stocks were mixed on Monday as oil prices retreated amid uncertainty over a proposed Russia-Ukraine energy truce, while investors prepared for a week of U.S. inflation data and third-quarter earnings.
Trading was thin on Monday, with Japan’s cash equity markets closed for Sports Day and U.S. bond markets shut for Columbus Day. U.S. stock exchanges remained open, while Treasury cash trading was suspended for the holiday.
Wall Street extended its record-setting week on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 0.6%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 0.8% and the Nasdaq Composite rising 0.6%, while Nasdaq 100 futures added 0.4% and S&P 500 futures climbed 0.3% in Asian trade.
Treasury yields reached their highest levels in 24 years last week, with the 10-year yield approaching 5.4%, while a gauge of U.S. investment-grade credit-default swaps climbed to its highest level since the Iran war began.
Markets are looking to U.S. consumer and producer inflation data and retail sales figures this week for clues on the Federal Reserve’s next moves.
Markets price an 18% chance of a Fed rate hike this month and an 85% probability of an increase in December.
Chip stocks mixed as TSMC earnings approach
South Korea’s KOSPI fell 2.6% as trading resumed after a long weekend. SK Hynix dropped 2.6%, Samsung Electronics lost 2.3% and LG Innotek plunged 13.1%.
Taiwan’s market also came under pressure, although individual suppliers diverged. Largan surged 7.9%, while Foxconn gained 2.6% and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing slipped 0.4%.
Investors are preparing for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing’s results on Thursday, when the world’s largest advanced-chip maker is expected to report a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings as demand for AI chips and advanced CoWoS packaging remains strong.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.3% and mainland China’s CSI 300 slipped 0.1% MiniMax gained 0.9%, NAURA Technology rose 0.4%, Cambricon Technologies added 1%, NetEase climbed 2.6%, Alibaba advanced 1.8% and Tencent gained 0.8%.
Meanwhile, China and the EU reached a 16-point consensus on trade, investment, export controls and intellectual property, with Beijing agreeing to curb hybrid-car exports as the bloc considers safeguard measures.
MAAS tumbles as Firmus IPO cancellation rattles AI investment
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.8%, but MAAS Group shares fell about 12%, extending last week’s selloff after AI data-centre operator Firmus scrapped its planned $5 billion initial public offering.
Oil prices also retreated after initially rising on renewed Middle East tensions. Brent crude fell 1.6% to $103.01 a barrel after reaching $105.63 earlier, while U.S. crude futures lost 1.9% to $90.11. Prices remain below a recent peak of $109.97.
The latest volatility followed weekend attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on shipping and Riyadh’s main airport, raising fears of a broader conflict and further disruption to energy supplies.
President Donald Trump’s claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire added to uncertainty. Neither side confirmed a finalized agreement, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no deal had been reached.
Trump’s proposal for Russia to increase diesel exports also drew objections from Republican and Democratic senators, who questioned whether it could be illegal.
Elsewhere, the S&P/ASX 200’s gain contrasted with declines across parts of Asia. New Zealand’s NZX 50 rose 0.4% to 13,801.22, Singapore’s Straits Times gained 0.7%, and Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite fell 0.5%. India’s Nifty 50 Futures climbed 1.4%.

By Wayne Cole
SYDNEY, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Stock markets got off to an erratic start on Monday as earnings season loomed, while oil slipped amid confusion over whether Russia would, or could, increase energy exports.
While the conflict in the Gulf continued with strikes on shipping and airports, President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia muddied the waters on oil supply.
Trump’s proposal for Russia to increase its exports of diesel added to the mix, though it also drew opposition from Republican and Democratic senators as potentially illegal.
Brent futures started higher but soon slipped 1.6% to $103.01 a barrel, below a recent top of $109.97, while US crude futures lost 1.9% to $90.11 a barrel. [O/R]
South Korean stocks fell 2.2% and Taiwanese shares eased 0.5%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan dipped 0.3%, while Chinese blue chips added 0.1%.
On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.3%, while Nasdaq futures firmed 0.4%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.5%, DAX futures gained 0.6% and FTSE futures added 0.4%.
Trade was thin with Japanese markets shut and the US on a partial holiday ahead of earnings season, with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday.
TSMC, the world’s largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips, will likely report a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings on Thursday.
S&P 500 earnings are expected to jump by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, though the bulk of that comes from the tech sector.
My Bui, an economist at AMP, said all the gains in the S&P 500 since mid-September had been in tech, while investors were demanding higher yields to fund the massive borrowing for AI.
The US investment-grade credit default swap index, which tracks the cost of insurance against default, had also risen sharply to its highest level since the US-Israeli war on Iran began.
"Overall, wider spreads suggest investors are questioning whether AI revenues can keep pace with rising borrowing costs," Bui said. "Corporate bond issuance to fund AI capex, combined with wider high-yield spreads, will raise refinancing costs as the current wave of debt matures over the next few years."
US CPI TO HEAT UP, BUT CORE COOLER
The flood of corporate debt has added to pressure in sovereign markets, driving Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week while lifting the discount applied to company earnings.
The market faces fresh challenges this week from US data on consumer and producer prices and retail sales. Rising energy costs are expected to lift CPI by a hefty 0.6% to an annual 3.7%, though the core is seen cooler at 0.2% and 2.5%.
"Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed as shipping costs have soared and product prices are even higher," said Bruce Kasman, head of global economics at JPMorgan.
"The signals on inflation point to a sharp rebound in headline inflation that will squeeze purchasing power and a firming in core inflation that will keep central banks focused on near-term hikes."
Markets imply only an 18% chance of a rate rise from the Federal Reserve this month, rising to an 85% chance of a hike in December. Investors are also wagering on hikes in the EU, Japan and Britain before the end of the year.
In currency markets, the euro remained on the defensive at $1.1201, having fallen for five weeks straight amid concerns about government deficits in Europe.
The dollar index held near 17-month highs at 102.25, but it has stalled on the yen at 158.19 as the threat of Japanese intervention deters speculators for now.
In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold rose 0.4% to $4,212 an ounce, having managed to bounce more than 1% last week. [GOL/]

title: Gold edges higher near $4,200 as traders weigh energy truce, Mideast risks
full_text:
8 emerging markets to consider in 2027: HSBC
Investing.com -- Gold prices edged higher on Monday as traders assessed U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim of an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine against renewed attacks in the Middle East that threatened to intensify inflation pressures.
At 20:30 ET (00:30 GMT), XAU/USD rose 0.3% to $4,206.86 an ounce after gaining 1.3% last week, while XAG/USD advanced 0.6% to $60.99. Platinum and palladium also moved higher. Benchmark Brent crude fell 1.2%.
Russia-Ukraine energy truce claim offsets Middle East risks
Trump said an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine had taken effect immediately, raising hopes of some relief for global fuel supplies.
He had previously urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and said Moscow had agreed to release diesel into global markets, potentially easing concerns over a fuel supply crunch.
However, renewed attacks in the Middle East continued to threaten energy security. Saudi Arabia’s main airport, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, came under attack from Houthi rebels on Sunday, a day after a strike on the facility killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
The Saturday attack was the deadliest incident in Saudi Arabia since the Iran war began in late February.
The Houthis described their attacks as retaliation for what they called Saudi aggression, including a strike on the airport in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. The latest violence has raised concerns that the conflict could spread further across the region, potentially pushing energy prices higher and strengthening the case for tighter monetary policy.
Although oil has eased, the precious metal has lost about a fifth of its value since the U.S.-Iran war erupted in late February.
Higher energy costs and the threat of broader inflation have prompted some central banks to raise interest rates, creating a headwind for gold because it does not generate interest income.
Central bank demand supports gold as rate risks persist
ANZ analysts said gold’s recent performance has been supported by rising investment demand, with inflows into gold-backed exchange-traded funds reaching a four-year high, according to Bloomberg data.
The analysts linked investor interest to mounting fiscal pressures around the world, particularly concerns about government debt-servicing costs and money supply. Central banks have also continued to increase their gold holdings.
The People’s Bank of China added 740,000 ounces to its reserves in September, extending its buying streak to 23 consecutive months.
However, ANZ cautioned that inflation risks could limit further gains if they prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten policy further. The prospect of higher interest rates remains a concern for gold, as yield-bearing assets become more attractive when borrowing costs rise.
Traders will therefore continue to weigh developments in the Russia-Ukraine conflict and Middle East energy flows against the outlook for inflation and monetary policy.

title: France’s bond stress may remain contained as wider European risks stay limited
full_text:
Investing.com -- France’s widening government bond spreads have revived memories of the euro zone debt crisis, but the stress remains concentrated in a handful of countries rather than signalling a broader deterioration across European markets, according to a market strategy note.
The assessment argues that France and Belgium are the region’s most vulnerable sovereign borrowers, but their underlying weaknesses remain less severe than those seen among stressed European economies during the 2011 debt crisis.
While some spillover is likely, the pressure may remain largely confined to France, limiting the need for a more aggressive response from the European Central Bank.
French bond spreads have returned to levels last seen during the euro zone debt crisis, but broader European stress indicators have yet to show comparable strain.
This distinction is important for investors assessing whether France’s fiscal and political difficulties could trigger a wider sell-off in European assets.
Belgium is seen as the next most vulnerable country, although the note argues that its risks, and those facing France, remain less pronounced than the vulnerabilities of weaker euro zone economies during the previous crisis.
Even so, the outlook for French bonds remains uncertain, with limited scope for meaningful relief ahead of the country’s election. Continued pressure on sovereign spreads could therefore leave the ECB unable to raise interest rates as aggressively as financial markets currently anticipate.
The strategy favours receiving ERZ7 against SFRZ7, a relative interest-rate position that reflects the view that the ECB may not deliver the full amount of tightening priced into markets. It also favours a weaker euro, recommending positions that sell the currency against a basket of Group of 10 currencies, where investor positioning is less stretched than against the U.S. dollar.
Despite the risks surrounding French debt, the strategy sees improving seasonal conditions for equities. U.S. stocks have yet to experience a meaningful pullback ahead of the U.S. midterm elections and the start of the Federal Reserve’s rate-hiking cycle, although valuations have contracted.
The most supportive seasonal period is expected in November and December, rather than immediately. The strategy therefore maintains a long position in U.S. equities while adding exposure to Brazil.
It has also added Brazilian equities and Brazilian government bonds due in 2031, known as NTNF 2031s, following what it describes as a very bullish election outcome. Lower interest rates are expected to act as a catalyst for both positions.
The broader investment outlook consequently hinges on whether sovereign stress in France remains contained, preventing a more aggressive ECB tightening cycle, while easing interest rates help support equity valuations and emerging-market assets.

title: China creates 10.52 million jobs, plans new AI and services employment measures
full_text:
8 emerging markets to consider in 2027: HSBC
Investing.com -- China created 10.52 million urban jobs in the first nine months of 2026, reaching 87.7% of its annual target, as Beijing announced plans to expand employment opportunities in artificial intelligence and the services sector.
The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security said on Saturday that employment conditions remained generally stable, with the surveyed urban unemployment rate averaging 5.2% between January and August.
Officials outlined initiatives aimed at supporting job creation, including a programme to help workers adapt their skills to advances in artificial intelligence.
The government also plans to introduce measures encouraging employment in the services sector, which authorities view as a major source of new jobs.
Vice Minister and ministry spokesperson Li Zhong said the government would work with other departments to develop a policy document promoting employment through services sector growth.
The initiative is intended to strengthen the sector’s role in absorbing workers across the economy.
Beijing will also seek to stabilise employment in labour-intensive industries and identify opportunities in emerging and future industries, Li said.
Other planned measures include additional employment support for university graduates and young people entering the workforce.
Authorities also intend to improve job quality for flexible workers and people employed through newer forms of work arrangements.
The announcements come as China seeks to balance technological development with employment stability, particularly as artificial intelligence reshapes workforce skills.
Officials also provided updated figures on the country’s social insurance programmes.
Basic pension insurance covered 1.079 billion people at the end of September, according to the ministry.
Unemployment insurance covered 251 million people, while work-injury insurance, including occupational-injury protection, covered 327 million.
The combined balance of China’s three social insurance funds stood at 11.2 trillion yuan ($1.67 trillion), the ministry said.
The latest employment figures leave China needing approximately 1.48 million additional urban jobs in the final quarter to meet its annual target of 12 million.

full_text:

By Wen-Yee Lee and Ben Blanchard
TAIPEI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - TSMC, the world’s largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips, will likely report a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings, driven by booming infrastructure spending in the tech sector.
Analysts say demand for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC) AI chipmaking capacity, as well as its advanced chip packaging technology, CoWoS, remains strong.
That has catapulted Asia’s most valuable company, a key supplier to Nvidia and Apple, to new heights. Its market capitalisation is almost double that of South Korean rival Samsung Electronics at around $2.1 trillion.
On Thursday, TSMC is expected to report a 65% surge in third-quarter net profit to T$746.3 billion ($23.4 billion), according to an LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts. SmartEstimates place greater weight on forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate.
An earnings call at which it will provide fourth-quarter and updated full-year guidance is scheduled for 0600 GMT.
Any result above T$706.56 billion would mark the company’s highest-ever quarterly net income, as well as its 11th consecutive quarter of profit growth.
Last Thursday, it posted a 50% year-on-year rise in third-quarter revenue, beating market forecasts and hitting a new record high.
In an October 6 report, Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan said he expected TSMC to raise its full-year revenue growth forecast to the low-to-mid 40% range from its current guidance of more than 40%, driven by strong demand for its 3-nanometre chips.
TEXAS EXPANSION PROSPECTS
TSMC is investing $265 billion to build chip factories in the US state of Arizona, including an additional $100 billion that was unveiled in July.
In September, Reuters reported that TSMC was evaluating a potential investment in Texas. Tesla CEO Elon Musk also said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing a part of it.
Analysts expect TSMC to address questions about its potential expansion plans in Texas.
In his report, Chan said an expansion in Texas could become necessary given growing customer demand and limited space at TSMC’s Arizona site in five years’ time.
Phelix Lee, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, however, saw limited urgency for TSMC to expand into Texas, given that some of its planned fabs in Arizona have yet to be built.
"Texas is a good location for a 2030s or 2040s expansion grand plan, given its long history of semiconductor ecosystem and talent pool," Lee said. "It may be a dangling carrot to preempt potential US trade and other policies."
On its July earnings call, the company raised its capex forecast for this year to between $60 billion and $64 billion from a previous prediction at the high end of $52 billion to $56 billion.
TSMC’s Taipei-listed shares have gained 63% so far this year, broadly in line with a 69% rise for the broader market.

title: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
full_text:

By Ali Sawafta, Nidal al-Mughrabi and Eman Abouhassira
RAMALLAH, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed legislative elections due next month until September 11, 2027, and called a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and the security situation in the Palestinian territories for the delay.
Abbas’ decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections", the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, pointing to the last Palestinian election having been held two decades ago, rejected Abbas’ remarks as "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead next month. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, after which Abbas’ rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.
The Palestinian Authority held municipal elections in April in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city in the enclave to participate. The vote was the first election held in Gaza since 2006.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel’s continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections this November.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
The decree called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to vote.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
Israel typically bans the Palestinian Authority from holding elections in East Jerusalem, territory it captured in the 1967 war and later annexed in a move most countries do not recognize.
The decision to postpone followed consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process.
PLEDGE TO HOLD VOTE AFTER TWO DECADES
Two Palestinian officials told Reuters on Thursday that leaders of Abbas’ Fatah movement and rival Hamas had agreed at a meeting in Cairo on Wednesday to postpone the elections.
An August poll by the West Bank-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) showed declining support for both Hamas and Fatah, which many Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank blame for their continuing political divisions.
The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed the November election timetable in his September 24 address to the UN General Assembly, as he sought to advance internationally backed reforms.
Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to hold presidential and legislative elections as part of France’s recognition of a Palestinian state in September 2025.
France’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that holding the elections was essential, and it welcomed the launch of an EU election observation mission.

A stronger headline reading could renew concerns that elevated energy prices are feeding into broader inflation. A softer core reading, meanwhile, could offer reassurance that underlying price pressures are easing.
Inflation affects how much room the Fed has to adjust interest rates. "The U.K. bond market is not risk-free, but the risk of a domestic catalyst for a gilt crisis has fallen," Barclays strategist Moyeen Islam said in a report prepared in partnership with the Institute for Fiscal Studies. The main immediate risks are more likely to come from international markets, he said.
Yields on 30-year gilts have risen to 5.9% from around 5.2% before last year’s Spring Forecast, and 10-year yields have climbed to 5.4% from 4.4%. But the roughly 0.6 percentage point rise in the 30-year yield is in line with, or slightly smaller than, the 0.7 to 1 point increases for comparable sovereign bonds.
Islam attributed the global rise mostly to expectations that inflation and central bank rates will climb and stay high after the Middle East conflict’s price shock. Markets imply U.K. inflation rising to 4.5% in early 2027 from just over 3%, staying higher for longer than in the U.S. or euro zone. Policy rates are priced to rise by at least 0.75 to 1 percentage point over the next 12 months in the UK, U.S. and euro zone.
The U.K.’s term premium, the extra compensation investors demand to hold longer-dated bonds, is elevated but has not risen materially in the past year. That suggests higher borrowing costs reflect policy rate expectations, not heightened concern over U.K. debt, Islam said.
Expectations for fiscal policy have also been stable, with surveys pointing to a deficit of about 3.3% of GDP in 2027 and 2.9% in 2028, in line with the Office for Budget Responsibility’s March forecast.
The backdrop remains difficult. U.K. debt stands at around 90% of national income, and debt interest costs of nearly 4% of national income are twice the average of the decade before COVID, Islam noted. The OBR’s March forecast already had the debt interest bill reaching £137 billion by 2030-31, and the upcoming forecast will revise it higher.
That leaves Chancellor John Healey, who will deliver his first Budget in a few weeks, with little room for error. Islam said it would be best for him to reaffirm the fiscal rules, with no discussion of flexibility or signs of creative fiscal accounting.
"For now, the focus of the bond market is on other countries, which is to the U.K.’s advantage," he wrote. "The government should try to keep it that way."

SHANGHAI/BEIJING, Oct 12 (Reuters) - China’s deal with the European Union to curb exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc is a fresh hit to Chinese EV makers that have ramped up hybrid shipments exempt from EU tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, as sales growth slows at home.
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU’s 27-member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of this year from $2.5 billion a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. The figure was nearly nine times the $845 million exported in all of 2021.
Since the EU imposed additional tariffs on Chinese-made EVs in 2024, Chinese automakers have increasingly turned to plug-in hybrids, which are exempt from the extra duties. Weak charging infrastructure in parts of Europe has also supported demand for plug-in hybrids, which are marketed for their long range and strong fuel economy.
SAIC, BYD and Chery accounted for more than 90% of Chinese hybrid sales volume in the EU, while hybrids represented more than half of their European sales, according to Jefferies.
"TARIFF RISK OFF, QUOTA RISK ON"
While European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on Friday the agreement would cut the imports of "several million cars over four years," Brussels and Beijing have yet to disclose how the arrangement will be implemented.
China’s Commerce Ministry said on Monday that the arrangement will allow continued export growth and guarantee China a quota no smaller than that granted to any other source of imports.
Investors largely viewed the agreement as a de-escalation of trade tensions and a sign that tariffs on Chinese hybrids may be off the table for now. Shares in BYD fell 1.8%, while Chery and SAIC rose 0.25% and 0.4%, respectively.
"Overall we believe it is a risk-relief rally story...as the implementation rules, volume caps, price floors, carve-outs are still pending technical negotiation," Citi analysts said.
The rapid growth of Chinese hybrid sales has increasingly challenged European manufacturers, including Volkswagen, long the region’s leading plug-in hybrid seller, said Li Yanwei, an analyst at the China Automobile Dealers Association.
BYD, China’s largest hybrid vehicle exporter to Europe, sold more plug-in hybrids than fully electric models in the first eight months of the year, with its Seal U SUV its best selling model, according to data compiled by Li.
Together with Chery, SAIC and Geely, the company has narrowed the gap with Volkswagen, which still commanded a 31.8% share of the EU plug-in hybrid market.
"Let’s see if China honours the agreement or finds workarounds, or temporary tariff exemptions," said Michael Dunne, a consultant who closely follows the Chinese automotive industry.
Analysts said the deal is set to expedite Chinese automakers’ move to increase production in Europe.
"I would expect this to strengthen the incentive for Chinese automakers to manufacture in Europe," said Bill Russo, founder of Shanghai-based consultancy Automobility.
"If access through imports becomes more constrained, investing closer to the customer becomes more attractive. But localisation requires capital...smaller players may reconsider their European ambitions."
Jefferies analysts said the deal signalled "tariff risk off, quota risk on," potentially pushing Chinese automakers towards higher-priced models, increasing pressure on German premium brands and accelerating plans to build more vehicles in Europe.

Investing.com -- A flood of new U.S. stock supply is likely to pressure valuations in 2027 but is not expected to derail the bull market, Goldman Sachs strategists say, as strong corporate and investor demand helps absorb it.
The team led by Ben Snider said 2026 is on track for record equity issuance. U.S. companies have raised $431 billion this year through IPOs, follow-ons, convertibles and SPACs, up 98% from a year earlier. The total will likely pass the prior high of $540 billion set in 2021, though the number of deals and issuance relative to market value are close to historical averages.
Activity has slowed since a record second quarter. Companies raised $93 billion in the third quarter, down from $252 billion in the second quarter, when half of the dollar volume came from two deals. The monthly number of offerings fell to about 50 on average from more than 90 in May and June.
Goldman linked the slowdown to a sharp rise in interest rates. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen about 125 basis points over the past year and more than 50 basis points since late August, moves of roughly two standard deviations. "Macro volatility, including the sharp recent increase in interest rates, has contributed to the slowdown in equity issuance," the strategists wrote.
Narrow market breadth has also hurt, with the median S&P 500 stock 16% below its high. "The strength of the S&P 500 has kept the Barometer at elevated levels. However, the median S&P 500 stock currently trades 16% below its respective high, pushing market breadth to its lowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble," they noted. "Incorporating this narrowness into the Barometer indicates IPO conditions that have recently softened and now rank slightly below the historical average."
For 2027, Goldman forecasts $600 billion of equity issuance, including $175 billion of IPOs, equal to 0.8% of U.S. equity market value, in line with the 10-year average. The bank expects solid growth, rising stock prices, lower interest rates and AI investment to drive it.
Equity is playing a supporting role in funding the AI boom. AI-related follow-on offerings have totaled $65 billion this year, or 45% of follow-on volume, compared with roughly $600 billion of AI-related debt issuance.
Demand, the strategists argue, should offset much of the supply. S&P 500 buybacks rose 15% in the first half, and Goldman expects gross buybacks of about $1.7 trillion in 2027, up from $1.5 trillion this year. With cash M&A, corporate equity demand should exceed $2 trillion. Households and foreign investors bought more than $1 trillion of stocks in the first half.
Including expiring lockups, net public equity supply will likely rise next year by the most since 2000. But Goldman said it is unrealistic to assume all unlocked shares will be sold immediately. "The shifting balance of corporate supply and demand adds pressure on equity valuations," the strategists said, "but we do not expect increasing equity supply to derail the bull market."

Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to get into the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation.

title: Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By Timour Azhari
RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before a series of deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300.
The government has not said why there were no alerts to the public before the four Riyadh attacks in the past week.
The warnings had served to highlight the violence undermining the kingdom’s efforts to project an image of calm to its people and the world during its war with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Their absence during the airport strikes raised questions about Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to attack and about its ability to protect residents and visitors, four Western and Arab officials in the region and political analysts told Reuters.
It also reflected efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, they said.
"They (the Saudi government) want to have it both ways: to launch a military operation and at the same time try to give confidence to the population and external stakeholders," said Sultan Alamer, a US-based Saudi academic and Senior Resident Fellow at the Middle East Policy Council think tank.
The Saudi civil defence - a national emergency management, rescue and firefighting agency which operates under the interior ministry and issues early warning alerts - and the Saudi government media office did not respond to emailed questions on why no alerts were issued.
Saudi Arabia’s approach is also one that some regional analysts said risked backfiring because the absence of warnings has heightened uncertainty in the kingdom.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence authority issued its first alerts since September 29, warning of potential threats in Riyadh and southern cities.
Reuters was unable to ascertain whether the decision to issue alerts again was a response to the airport attacks, and the Saudi government did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.
SYSTEM GOES SILENT
All Gulf countries have been hit by Iranian drones and missiles since the US-Iran war began in February, but their governments have handled public warnings differently.
Qatar’s interior ministry has issued mobile phone alerts before nearly every attack, including most recent attacks in July, when residents were warned to stay inside and away from windows.
Bahrain and Kuwait have repeatedly sounded sirens urging people to take shelter.
Saudi Arabia began issuing threat alerts to mobile phones and social media accounts via a national early warning system in May. But despite increasing Houthi attacks leading up to last week, the system went silent.
The last alert before last week’s attacks was issued on September 29, for the southern province of Najran, according to posts on the civil defence X account.
The civil defences authority has continued to issue warnings about staying out of harm’s way during adverse weather, including rain and flooding, and did so as recently as Monday.
It also warned residents not to share images, rumours or information about interceptions and impact sites, including in a post on Monday, under government regulations issued in March.
Reuters could not determine whether anyone had faced prosecution for sharing such information, and the Saudi government media office did not respond to a request for comment on the matter.
Before last week’s airport attacks, officials from an allied Western government asked Saudi authorities why the alerts had stopped, two officials with direct knowledge of the matter said.
The response was that the alerts were too disruptive and many citizens had complained they were being woken by them at night, the officials said.
The Saudi government media office and Saudi officials did not respond to requests for comment on the assertion.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh was trying to balance public messaging on attacks with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but had ended up adding to a sense of unease about the strikes.
"Their approach to public messaging seems like a corollary to the quandary they are in: They need to respond to the Houthis but don’t want that to result in societal disruption and their public messaging is a reflection of that," he said.
"But the lack of alerts of incoming Houthi attacks creates the very nervousness they are trying to avoid."
NEW THREAT ALERT
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst close to the government, said that with or without early warnings, the kingdom would struggle to defend all of its assets because of its size.
"In Saudi Arabia you have too much to protect. It’s a huge country with airports, pipelines and oil facilities. There is just not enough coverage to defend everything at once, not enough Patriots (missile defence systems), interceptors and missile batteries to do it all," he said.
"Saudi Arabia has an unlimited need for air defences," he added."
Despite the attacks, Saudi Arabia hosted an international conference on Monday, though major oil bosses dropped out.
At the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh, Saudi Prince Abdulaziz bin Salaman, a brother of the Saudi crown prince and the kingdom’s energy minister, struck a defiant tone while acknowledging risks and Saudi Arabia’s intent to keep its economic plans on track. He thanked all who had travelled to Riyadh "because you know this country is safe" but added: "Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone." "We will never forfeit any chance to maintain our commitment and our vision," he said.
EMBASSIES ISSUE THEIR OWN INTERNAL ALERTS
Despite no public alerts being issued this month until Monday, Riyadh has been attacked about a dozen times, two of the Western officials said.
During that time, Western embassies in the kingdom have been issuing their own internal missile and drone alerts to staff, according to three people familiar with the matter and alerts seen by Reuters.
These internal alerts are compiled from a mixture of US and other Western government intelligence and input from Saudi authorities, one of those people said.
They include alerts sent to staff around the time of two first airport strikes last week according to the people familiar with the matter.
They said that even the embassies had received no internal warning before Saturday’s airport strike, without offering an explanation.
Reuters could not determine why no warning came before Saturday’s attack, the deadliest of last week’s attacks.
On Sunday, Saudi state TV released footage of Saturday’s strike.
It showed several shots of travellers in the airport terminal. Dozens lined up to board a flight. Men and women sat in chairs waiting, their eyes trained on the screens of their mobile phones as they scrolled.
Then, the bright orange flash of a missile explosion.

title: UK shoppers stay cautious as fuel costs bite, surveys show
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
Oct 13 (Reuters) - British consumers kept a lid on spending in September, with much of their extra outlay going on fuel, while warm weather helped pubs but hurt clothing sales, according to surveys published on Tuesday.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC) trade body said its total retail sales measure rose by 1.3% compared with a year ago, picking up from 0.7% in August but below its 12-month average of 1.5%.
A separate survey from Barclays, based on consumer card spending data, showed a 2.0% annual increase in September, slowing from August’s 2.1% rise.
It pointed to a rise in households’ confidence around their finances but also some nerves ahead of finance minister John Healey’s budget on October 28.
Here are the key points from the two surveys:
• The BRC said Food sales were up by 2.5% while non-food sales edged up by 0.3%
• Health and beauty had its strongest month of the year so far and toys were boosted by Pokemon’s 30th anniversary products, but clothing and footwear had a weak month due to unseasonably warm weather
• "Retail sales growth remained subdued in September as households are still cautious with their spending ahead of expected rises in household bills and taxes," said BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson
• Barclays said essential spending was up by 2.5%, driven by a 17.3% jump in fuel spending after diesel prices hit record highs, while non-essential spending edged up by 1.8%
• Bars, pubs and clubs reported a 3.8% rise in spending, their fourth straight month of growth, as summer weather extended through most of September
• Barclays’ measure of confidence in household finances rose to a seven-month high of 67%, but 68% of consumers said they were concerned about the budget’s impact on their finances and 30% said they were cutting back on non-essential spending
• The BRC survey covered the period of August 30-October 3 while the Barclays spending data was August 22-September 24

title: NYT, Economist among publishers joining coalition to curb unpaid AI use
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
Oct 12 (Reuters) - The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission.
The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil’s National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press.
Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier this month, USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement.
OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organizations, including the New York Times.
SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website.
"Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist," Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times’ head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement.
Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites.
Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat.
SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardize how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work.

title: Kroger plans to eliminate 3,000 corporate roles, memo shows, as it expands AI use
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
Oct 12 (Reuters) - Kroger plans to cut roughly 3,000 corporate roles over the next three years, CEO Greg Foran told staff in a memo, seen by Reuters on Monday, as the grocer integrates AI into its workflow.
Kroger should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, Foran wrote in the memo, adding that the job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees.
Foran took over as Kroger’s CEO in February.
Companies have been rethinking corporate structures and cutting jobs as they increasingly turn to AI to streamline workflows and divert more resources toward the technology, fuelling concerns over widespread disruption across sectors.
Last month the company outlined the company’s AI strategy, including the use of models to manage workflows and leverage customer data to power tools such as its AI shopping assistant.
The grocery retailer had also lowered its annual identical sales target and said it is seeking to cut prices to better compete with rivals such as Walmart and Aldi as consumers grow more frugal under pressure from high gas prices.
Details on the job cuts, which would affect about 37% of its 8,200 corporate employees, would be shared in the coming months, Foran said in the memo.
Bloomberg News first reported on the job cuts on Monday.
In June last year, the company cut about 1,000 corporate roles.
